questions.question: During evaluation of palpitations, continuous ECG shows a regular narrow-complex rhythm gradually accelerating from 90 to 135/min as fever rises. P-wave morphology and axis match the baseline sinus tracing, and the rate falls gradually after treatment of fever and dehydration. Which mechanism best fits?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Physiological sinus tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Sinus Tachycardia Versus Paroxysmal Reentrant SVT

Correct answer: Physiological sinus tachycardia

Interpret the Whole Rate Trajectory

**Sinus tachycardia is usually a response to increased demand or altered autonomic drive.** Fever, hypovolemia, pain, hypoxemia, anemia, thyrotoxicosis and other triggers should be sought according to the presentation.

A sinus-appearing P wave before each QRS, appropriate atrial axis and gradual acceleration or deceleration support the diagnosis. Comparison with the baseline tracing is useful when morphology is uncertain.

Atrial and ventricular rates alone do not define the mechanism. Sinus tachycardia can be rapid, while AVNRT or AVRT can be relatively slow under medication or in older patients.

Treat the Driver Before Suppressing the Rate

**Correct the physiological cause and reassess perfusion and symptoms.** Tachycardia may be compensatory, so reflex AV-nodal blockade can worsen output in a depleted or critically ill patient.

Reentrant SVTs typically have abrupt onset and termination, whereas automatic focal AT may show warm-up and cool-down. These are clues that require integration with atrial morphology and a recorded episode.

Inappropriate sinus tachycardia is considered only when a persistent symptomatic sinus-rate syndrome is not explained by a physiological or secondary cause. A febrile dehydrated patient does not meet that interpretation simply because the resting rate exceeds 100/min. POTS requires a posture-related assessment and its own criteria rather than a fever-associated tracing. Obtain a 12-lead ECG during symptoms when feasible and reconsider the mechanism if episodes remain abrupt or unexplained after the trigger resolves.

Focal atrial tachycardia: An automatic atrial focus can warm up and cool down, so gradual change alone is not diagnostic. Here the unchanged sinus morphology and rate response to a documented physiological demand favor sinus tachycardia rather than a non-sinus focus.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT commonly starts and stops abruptly and often obscures atrial activity within or near the QRS. Gradual rate change with a physiological trigger and unchanged sinus P waves supports sinus activation instead.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Orthodromic AVRT usually has abrupt paroxysms and retrograde atrial activation associated with a circuit using the AV node and an accessory pathway. The observed gradual sinus-rate trajectory is less consistent with that mechanism.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A patient has abrupt recurrent regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 185/min. Retrograde atrial deflections appear just after the QRS with a very short RP interval. The baseline ECG has no delta wave. Which interpretation is most defensible before electrophysiological confirmation?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia is established by a visible atrial deflection
Orthodromic AVRT is excluded by the normal baseline ECG
Typical AVNRT is favored, but orthodromic AVRT through a concealed pathway remains possible
Typical atrial flutter is established by the ventricular rate
questions.explanation:
Short-RP Regular Narrow-Complex Tachycardia

Correct answer: Typical AVNRT is favored, but orthodromic AVRT through a concealed pathway remains possible

RP Timing Narrows the Differential

**A very short RP interval during abrupt regular SVT favors typical slow–fast AVNRT.** Near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation can hide retrograde P waves or produce a pseudo-r-prime in V1 or pseudo-S waves inferiorly.

Orthodromic AVRT uses antegrade AV nodal/His–Purkinje conduction and retrograde accessory-pathway conduction. Its retrograde P wave may also lie shortly after the QRS, so surface timing is not an infallible circuit diagnosis.

A concealed pathway conducts retrogradely without manifest antegrade pre-excitation. A normal sinus-rhythm ECG therefore cannot independently exclude accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia.

Use the Recording to Guide Further Assessment

**Preserve a 12-lead tracing during tachycardia and compare it with sinus rhythm.** Examine regularity, QRS width, atrial activation and onset or termination rather than relying on a rate label.

Vagal maneuvers or adenosine can terminate AV-node-dependent circuits in a suitable stable patient. Termination supports nodal dependence but does not alone distinguish AVNRT from AVRT, and some focal tachycardias can also respond.

EPS can establish the mechanism when recurrent symptoms justify definitive assessment or ablation. Initial management still depends on hemodynamic stability and the actual rhythm: a diagnostic hypothesis must not delay treatment of attributable shock. Explain that the likely diagnosis can be clinically useful without pretending that a short-RP strip uniquely identifies every circuit. The eventual ablation target differs between an AV nodal slow pathway and an accessory pathway, making precise mechanism assessment consequential.

Focal atrial tachycardia is established by a visible atrial deflection: Visible atrial activity occurs in several SVTs, including retrograde activation during AVNRT or AVRT. Its timing, morphology and response to diagnostic maneuvers matter more than visibility alone.

Orthodromic AVRT is excluded by the normal baseline ECG: An accessory pathway that conducts only retrogradely can support orthodromic AVRT without producing a delta wave in sinus rhythm. Absence of manifest pre-excitation therefore does not exclude this circuit.

Typical atrial flutter is established by the ventricular rate: Flutter with 2:1 conduction often produces a rate near 150/min, but rates vary and rate alone is not diagnostic. The supplied tracing does not demonstrate a continuing flutter cycle or additional atrial waves.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A stable patient has regular narrow-complex tachycardia with RP longer than PR and negative P waves in the inferior leads. Adenosine terminates the episode. Which conclusion is most defensible from these findings alone?
options: Negative inferior P waves establish permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia
Adenosine termination establishes atypical AVNRT
Atypical AVNRT, slowly conducting-pathway AVRT and adenosine-sensitive atrial tachycardia remain possible
RP longer than PR establishes focal atrial tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Long-RP Supraventricular Tachycardia

Correct answer: Atypical AVNRT, slowly conducting-pathway AVRT and adenosine-sensitive atrial tachycardia remain possible

Delayed Atrial Timing Has Several Mechanisms

**Long-RP tachycardia describes atrial activation late after the preceding QRS, with RP longer than the following PR.** It does not by itself establish whether atrial activity drives or follows the ventricular cycle.

Fast–slow or slow–slow AVNRT can have delayed retrograde nodal activation. PJRT is orthodromic AVRT using a slowly conducting, decremental retrograde accessory pathway, commonly producing inferiorly negative P waves.

A focal atrial source can produce a similar apparent relationship. Sinus tachycardia and other junctional mechanisms remain relevant in the appropriate clinical context; onset, offset and atrial morphology help refine the assessment.

Adenosine Response Is Not a Mechanism Label

**Adenosine termination is compatible with more than one long-RP circuit.** AV-node-dependent reentry can stop, while certain adenosine-sensitive focal atrial mechanisms can also terminate.

Record the full termination sequence and determine whether atrial activity persists when ventricular conduction is interrupted. EPS can resolve the mechanism when recurrent symptoms or an ablation decision make certainty consequential.

Incessant long-RP tachycardia can cause tachycardia-mediated ventricular dysfunction, particularly with PJRT or incessant AT. Evaluate burden and ventricular function rather than assuming a modest rate makes it harmless. Treatment and ablation targets differ between a slow nodal pathway, an accessory pathway and an atrial focus. Avoid applying a definitive procedural label from one P-wave polarity or an adenosine response; preserve the working differential until sufficient evidence is available.

Mechanism | Reason for long RP | Important qualification

Atypical AVNRT | Delayed retrograde nodal activation | Inferiorly negative P waves can resemble PJRT

PJRT | Slow decremental retrograde accessory pathway | No baseline delta wave is required

Focal AT | Atrial focus with its own activation timing | Some forms terminate with adenosine

Negative inferior P waves establish permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia: PJRT often has long RP and inferiorly negative retrograde P waves, but atypical AVNRT and low atrial foci can resemble this pattern. Additional electrophysiological evidence is needed before assigning that specific pathway mechanism.

Adenosine termination establishes atypical AVNRT: Atypical AVNRT can terminate with adenosine, but slowly conducting accessory-pathway AVRT and some focal AT mechanisms can do so as well. The drug response is not a unique circuit identifier.

RP longer than PR establishes focal atrial tachycardia: Focal AT is an important long-RP diagnosis, but delayed retrograde conduction during atypical AVNRT or AVRT can produce the same surface timing relationship. RP classification narrows rather than completes the differential.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: During a regular narrow-complex tachycardia, adenosine causes several nonconducted atrial impulses. Discrete abnormal P waves continue at the same cycle length, separated by an isoelectric baseline, and one-to-one ventricular conduction then resumes. Which interpretation best fits the observed response?
options: An atrial tachycardia continuing independently of transient AV nodal block
Orthodromic AVRT continuing through the blocked AV node
Sinus tachycardia established by adenosine resistance
Typical AVNRT established by resumption of one-to-one conduction
questions.explanation:
Adenosine Unmasks Continuing Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: An atrial tachycardia continuing independently of transient AV nodal block

Inspect the Atria During the Ventricular Pause

**Adenosine can reveal atrial activity by transiently reducing AV conduction.** A continuing organized atrial rhythm may become visible when fewer QRS complexes obscure it.

Discrete abnormal P waves with intervening isoelectric segments support focal AT in the appropriate context. Flutter can also persist during AV block, but typically shows a macroreentrant atrial pattern; surface appearance is not infallible, especially with scar-related rhythms.

The atrial cycle length and activation pattern provide the diagnostic information. Merely observing a short ventricular pause or a lower displayed heart rate does not prove that the tachycardia terminated.

Interpret AV Block With Appropriate Limits

**Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs antegrade conduction through the AV node.** Interruption usually stops that circuit, whereas an atrial rhythm can continue and later regain ventricular conduction.

AVNRT can occasionally persist despite block in an output pathway, so ventricular block by itself is not an absolute exclusion of every nodal circuit. Integrate the atrial recording, timing and other electrophysiological evidence.

Some focal ATs terminate with adenosine; others merely become easier to identify. Preserve the diagnostic strip and choose subsequent treatment according to the actual rhythm, symptoms, burden and ventricular function. Do not repeatedly escalate adenosine simply because a continuing atrial rhythm fails to terminate. For recurrent or incessant symptomatic focal AT, specialist evaluation and ablation can be appropriate. Acute hemodynamic compromise still requires immediate rhythm-directed management rather than prolonged diagnostic drug challenges.

Orthodromic AVRT continuing through the blocked AV node: The AV node is the antegrade limb of ordinary orthodromic AVRT. Sustained atrial activity at an unchanged cycle despite interruption of that limb argues against this circuit as the explanation.

Sinus tachycardia established by adenosine resistance: Sinus activity can continue during transient AV block, but adenosine resistance does not establish sinus origin. The abnormal discrete P-wave morphology supports a non-sinus atrial source in this recording.

Typical AVNRT established by resumption of one-to-one conduction: AVNRT can rarely continue with block below its circuit, so absent ventricular responses alone do not settle every case. Here the independently continuing discrete abnormal atrial rhythm favors AT, and resumption of conduction is not proof of nodal reentry.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

questions.question: A patient has repeated narrow-complex tachycardia at 140–160/min. Each episode has one consistent P-wave morphology different from sinus rhythm, with an isoelectric interval between P waves. The atrial rate gradually accelerates at onset, and occasional AV block occurs without changing atrial timing. Which diagnosis is most likely?
options: Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Focal atrial tachycardia
questions.explanation:
Focal Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: Focal atrial tachycardia

Recognize an Organized Non-Sinus Atrial Rhythm

**Focal AT produces atrial activation spreading from a localized source.** Discrete P waves differing from sinus morphology, often with intervening isoelectric segments, support the diagnosis.

Automatic activity can show warm-up and cool-down. Triggered activity and localized reentry are other mechanisms, so a focal ECG appearance does not prove that every such tachycardia is automatic.

The ventricular response depends on AV conduction and may be slower or irregular despite an organized atrial rhythm. Continuing atrial activity during AV block helps separate the atrial driver from an ordinary AVRT circuit.

Assess Burden and Select Treatment

**Incessant or frequently recurrent AT can cause tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy.** Assess symptoms, duration, ventricular function and reversible triggers instead of judging severity from one rate measurement.

Acute treatment depends on stability and mechanism. Adenosine can terminate some focal ATs or expose atrial activity without termination. Beta blockade or verapamil/diltiazem may help selected stable patients, with attention to hypotension, ventricular function and contraindications.

Catheter ablation is an important definitive option for recurrent symptomatic focal AT, particularly incessant AT associated with ventricular dysfunction. Mapping identifies the source; P-wave morphology offers clues but cannot replace invasive localization when ablation is performed. Atrial scarring can complicate the ECG distinction from macroreentry, and an isoelectric interval is not absolute proof against flutter. Reassess ventricular function after rhythm control when tachycardia-mediated dysfunction is suspected; improvement supports the causal contribution but does not exclude additional myocardial disease.

Multifocal atrial tachycardia: MAT has changing P-wave morphologies and irregular atrial timing. A single reproducible non-sinus morphology with an organized atrial cycle instead supports a single dominant atrial activation source.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: Typical AVNRT usually has abrupt onset and near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation. Persistent independent abnormal atrial activity and warm-up favor an atrial source rather than that usual nodal circuit.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs AV conduction as part of its circuit. Continued atrial tachycardia through AV block, together with non-sinus P waves and gradual acceleration, supports a focal atrial mechanism.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

Focal Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: D — Focal atrial tachycardia

Recognize an Organized Non-Sinus Atrial Rhythm

  • Focal AT produces atrial activation spreading from a localized source. Discrete P waves differing from sinus morphology, often with intervening isoelectric segments, support the diagnosis.
    • Automatic activity can show warm-up and cool-down. Triggered activity and localized reentry are other mechanisms, so a focal ECG appearance does not prove that every such tachycardia is automatic.
    • The ventricular response depends on AV conduction and may be slower or irregular despite an organized atrial rhythm. Continuing atrial activity during AV block helps separate the atrial driver from an ordinary AVRT circuit.

Assess Burden and Select Treatment

  • Incessant or frequently recurrent AT can cause tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy. Assess symptoms, duration, ventricular function and reversible triggers instead of judging severity from one rate measurement.
    • Acute treatment depends on stability and mechanism. Adenosine can terminate some focal ATs or expose atrial activity without termination. Beta blockade or verapamil/diltiazem may help selected stable patients, with attention to hypotension, ventricular function and contraindications.
    • Catheter ablation is an important definitive option for recurrent symptomatic focal AT, particularly incessant AT associated with ventricular dysfunction. Mapping identifies the source; P-wave morphology offers clues but cannot replace invasive localization when ablation is performed. Atrial scarring can complicate the ECG distinction from macroreentry, and an isoelectric interval is not absolute proof against flutter. Reassess ventricular function after rhythm control when tachycardia-mediated dysfunction is suspected; improvement supports the causal contribution but does not exclude additional myocardial disease.

Other Options

  • A — Multifocal atrial tachycardia: MAT has changing P-wave morphologies and irregular atrial timing. A single reproducible non-sinus morphology with an organized atrial cycle instead supports a single dominant atrial activation source.
  • B — Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: Typical AVNRT usually has abrupt onset and near-simultaneous atrial and ventricular activation. Persistent independent abnormal atrial activity and warm-up favor an atrial source rather than that usual nodal circuit.
  • C — Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs AV conduction as part of its circuit. Continued atrial tachycardia through AV block, together with non-sinus P waves and gradual acceleration, supports a focal atrial mechanism.

References

  • ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019

questions.question: During an exacerbation of COPD, a patient has an irregular narrow-complex rhythm at 125/min. A single lead shows at least three distinct P-wave morphologies, variable P–P and PR intervals, and isoelectric segments between atrial deflections. Which diagnosis best fits?

Atrial fibrillation
Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction

questions.explanation:
Multifocal Atrial Tachycardia

Correct answer: Multifocal atrial tachycardia

Use Atrial Morphology to Explain the Irregularity

**MAT is a rapid irregular atrial rhythm with at least three distinct P-wave morphologies in the same lead.** The conventional rate distinction from wandering atrial pacemaker is ==greater than 100/min==.

P–P, PR and R–R intervals can vary, while recognizable atrial depolarizations remain separated by isoelectric segments. Confirm that artefact or superimposed T waves are not being counted as extra morphologies.

Pulmonary disease, hypoxemia, pulmonary hypertension, electrolyte disturbances and theophylline exposure are relevant associations. The clinical setting supports the diagnosis but does not replace the ECG criteria.

Treat the Underlying Illness First

**Correct the precipitating respiratory or systemic disorder and potassium or magnesium abnormalities.** Review potentially contributory drugs while maintaining adequate treatment of the underlying pulmonary disease.

IV magnesium can be useful even when the measured level is normal. If symptomatic rapid conduction persists, selected beta blockers or verapamil/diltiazem can slow the ventricular response; choose according to bronchospasm, pressure, LV function and other contraindications.

Electrical cardioversion and conventional rhythm drugs generally do not provide durable control of this multifocal atrial process. MAT alone does not establish the AF-related indication for anticoagulation; look for any separate indication rather than treating every irregular pulse as AF. Follow clinical recovery and repeat the ECG when needed. Persistent drug-refractory tachycardia with associated ventricular dysfunction warrants specialist assessment, while an acute pulmonary trigger should not lead directly to invasive treatment without an attempt to correct that driver.

Rhythm | Atrial finding | Timing clue

MAT | At least 3 discrete P morphologies in one lead | Irregular P–P; rate >100/min

Wandering atrial pacemaker | Multiple discrete P morphologies | Similar pattern at a slower rate

AF | No consistent discrete P sequence | Irregular ventricular response unless another mechanism intervenes

Flutter with variable block | Repeating organized atrial activation | Irregular ventricular conduction with organized atrial cycle

Atrial fibrillation: AF has disorganized atrial activation without consistently identifiable discrete P waves. Irregularity alone is insufficient: the multiple discrete P morphologies and intervening isoelectric baseline support MAT.

Atrial flutter with variable AV conduction: Variable conduction can make flutter ventricular intervals irregular, but the underlying atrial cycle is usually organized and repetitive. Changing P-wave morphologies and irregular atrial intervals favor MAT.

Sinus tachycardia with frequent atrial premature beats: Sinus rhythm with ectopy retains a dominant sinus sequence interrupted by premature beats. A sustained irregular atrial rhythm with several recurring morphologies and no dominant sinus cycle is more consistent with MAT.

questions.question: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia runs at 150/min. During a monitored diagnostic maneuver, ventricular conduction briefly slows and continuous atrial activity at 300/min becomes visible, with repetitive negative deflections in the inferior leads. Which diagnosis best explains the original rhythm?
options: Focal atrial tachycardia with one-to-one conduction
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Atrial flutter with two-to-one AV conduction
questions.explanation:
Atrial Flutter With Concealed Two-to-One Conduction

Correct answer: Atrial flutter with two-to-one AV conduction

Find the Hidden Atrial Cycle

**Flutter with 2:1 conduction can masquerade as a regular SVT because alternate atrial deflections are concealed by QRS or T waves.** A ventricular rate near 150/min is a useful prompt to inspect the atria, not a diagnostic criterion by itself.

The usual atrial rate is approximately 250–330/min, but medications, scarring and other substrates can change it. Determine the actual atrial rate rather than assuming that every flutter cycle is exactly 200 ms.

Counterclockwise typical flutter often produces negative inferior flutter waves and positive activity in V1. Surface morphology suggests but does not definitively establish cavotricuspid-isthmus dependence.

Diagnostic Slowing Does Not Necessarily Terminate Flutter

**Transient AV nodal block may reveal the atrial rhythm while the macroreentrant circuit continues.** Record the full tracing to distinguish ventricular slowing from conversion to sinus rhythm.

Adenosine is not routine curative treatment for flutter. When used diagnostically in uncertainty, it requires monitoring and rescue readiness because AF induction or rebound rapid conduction can occur.

After recognition, assess stability, ventricular function, episode duration and thromboembolic protection before choosing rate control, cardioversion or ablation. Flutter may be difficult to rate-control, and typical flutter often responds well to CTI ablation. A successful flutter intervention does not eliminate later AF or automatically end anticoagulation requirements. The immediate diagnostic lesson is to count atrial events during slowed conduction; rate labels alone can miss the rhythm that determines subsequent treatment.

Focal atrial tachycardia with one-to-one conduction: Focal AT can continue through AV block, but one-to-one conduction would not explain the original atrial-to-ventricular ratio of two. Continuous repetitive flutter activity further favors macroreentry over a discrete focal P-wave pattern.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: AVNRT can obscure atrial activity near the QRS, but the newly visible atrial cycle is twice the original ventricular rate and continues independently as conduction slows. This supports an atrial driver rather than ordinary one-to-one nodal reentry.

Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT requires atria and ventricles in its circuit. A continuing atrial rhythm at 300/min while the ventricular response slows is inconsistent with the usual one-to-one accessory-pathway circuit.

questions.explanation:
Nonreentrant Junctional Tachycardia

Correct answer: Enhanced automaticity producing focal junctional tachycardia

Recognize a Junctional Driver

**Focal junctional tachycardia arises from abnormal impulse formation near the AV node or proximal His region.** A narrow QRS rhythm with AV dissociation can occur because the junctional rate exceeds the sinus rate.

Warm-up and cool-down favor an automatic mechanism over abrupt reentry. Some cases have retrograde atrial conduction, even one-to-one, which can make the surface rhythm resemble AVNRT or AVRT.

AV dissociation rules out ordinary AVRT but does not absolutely exclude every AVNRT variant. A careful mechanism assessment is therefore more reliable than using a single surface sign as universal proof.

Address the Context and Hemodynamic Consequences

**Assess postoperative stress, catecholamine exposure, ischemia, electrolyte disturbance and medication toxicity.** The setting and ventricular function influence both urgency and treatment.

Treat reversible drivers and obtain specialist rhythm input. Selected beta blockers or other antiarrhythmics can be used according to the clinical substrate; evidence in adults is limited, and a pediatric postoperative regimen should not be transferred automatically.

Adenosine may reveal atrial nonparticipation but does not reliably terminate automatic junctional tachycardia. Electrical cardioversion is also less likely to provide durable suppression of an automatic focus than of a reentrant circuit. Persistent symptomatic or hemodynamically important disease can require specialized treatment, including selected ablation with attention to AV-block risk. Avoid reflexly selecting slow-pathway ablation merely because the rhythm arises near the AV junction; the target and procedural risks depend on the demonstrated mechanism.

Focal atrial tachycardia with variable AV block: Focal AT requires the rapid driver to be atrial. Here the atrial rate is slower than the ventricular rhythm and independent of it, so the atria are not supplying the tachycardic impulse sequence.

Orthodromic AV reentry through an accessory pathway: Ordinary orthodromic AVRT needs the atria and ventricles as circuit components. Sustained tachycardia with independent slower atrial activity argues against that mechanism rather than an accessory-pathway return limb.

Typical slow–fast AV nodal reentry: AVNRT is a reentrant mechanism, usually with abrupt onset and offset. Although rare AVNRT variants can dissociate the atria, gradual rate behavior and the postoperative context favor automatic junctional tachycardia here.

questions.question: An adult develops abrupt regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 210/min, followed immediately by BP 68/40 mmHg, confusion and cool extremities. A pulse is present. Pads are attached and synchronized cardioversion is available. Which next strategy is best?
options: Complete several attempts at vagal maneuvers before preparing cardioversion
Perform prompt synchronized cardioversion with concurrent resuscitative support
Give IV diltiazem and await its full effect before cardioversion
Give a full escalating adenosine sequence before deciding on cardioversion
questions.explanation:
Unstable Regular Narrow-Complex Tachycardia

Correct answer: Perform prompt synchronized cardioversion with concurrent resuscitative support

Establish That the Rhythm Is Causing Compromise

**A tachyarrhythmia with a pulse requires urgent synchronized cardioversion when it causes hemodynamic instability.** Hypotension, acute altered mentation, shock, ischemic discomfort or acute HF are clinically important manifestations.

The abrupt rhythm change followed by circulatory deterioration supports causation here. Sinus tachycardia accompanying sepsis or hypovolemia requires treatment of its driver rather than cardioversion simply because the patient is unstable.

A numerical heart-rate threshold is not an independent rule. Assess pulse, rhythm and perfusion together, and support airway, ventilation and circulation while preparing treatment.

Deliver a Synchronized Shock Safely

**Synchronization times the shock to ventricular depolarization to reduce the risk of delivering energy during vulnerable repolarization.** Confirm synchronization markers on the QRS and recheck after each attempt because some devices reset the mode.

Use the device-recommended energy or the relevant 2025 rhythm-specific guidance; the AHA 2025 algorithm specifies the maximum energy setting if the recommended setting is unknown. Escalate appropriately if unsuccessful. Provide sedation when feasible, but do not postpone necessary treatment in a rapidly deteriorating patient to complete elective sedation steps.

Adenosine is a possible immediate adjunct for a regular narrow rhythm, not permission to delay available cardioversion through prolonged pharmacological trials. Unsynchronized defibrillation follows a different pathway, including VF or pulseless VT; reassess immediately if the pulse is lost. After conversion, obtain a diagnostic ECG, review reversible causes and document the arrhythmia for definitive evaluation. Successful conversion treats the episode but does not establish the precise reentrant circuit or remove the need to address recurrence.

Complete several attempts at vagal maneuvers before preparing cardioversion: Vagal maneuvers are appropriate initial treatment for suitable stable regular SVT. Persistent profound shock and altered mentation attributable to the rhythm make repeated attempts an inappropriate reason to delay cardioversion.

Give IV diltiazem and await its full effect before cardioversion: Diltiazem can treat selected stable narrow-complex tachycardias. In severe hypotension it can further compromise pressure, and waiting for drug effect delays definitive treatment of the unstable rhythm.

Give a full escalating adenosine sequence before deciding on cardioversion: Adenosine can be considered for regular narrow-complex tachycardia while immediate cardioversion is being arranged. Completing an escalating sequence is not a prerequisite when profound instability persists and cardioversion is ready.

AHA adult advanced life support guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001376

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

explanationTeaching.title: Unstable Regular Narrow-Complex Tachycardia

sections.heading: Establish That the Rhythm Is Causing Compromise

bullets.text: **A tachyarrhythmia with a pulse requires urgent synchronized cardioversion when it causes hemodynamic instability.** Hypotension, acute altered mentation, shock, ischemic discomfort or acute HF are clinically important manifestations.
children: The abrupt rhythm change followed by circulatory deterioration supports causation here. Sinus tachycardia accompanying sepsis or hypovolemia requires treatment of its driver rather than cardioversion simply because the patient is unstable.
A numerical heart-rate threshold is not an independent rule. Assess pulse, rhythm and perfusion together, and support airway, ventilation and circulation while preparing treatment.

sections.heading: Deliver a Synchronized Shock Safely

bullets.text: **Synchronization times the shock to ventricular depolarization to reduce the risk of delivering energy during vulnerable repolarization.** Confirm synchronization markers on the QRS and recheck after each attempt because some devices reset the mode.
children: Use the device-recommended energy or the relevant 2025 rhythm-specific guidance; the AHA 2025 algorithm specifies the maximum energy setting if the recommended setting is unknown. Escalate appropriately if unsuccessful. Provide sedation when feasible, but do not postpone necessary treatment in a rapidly deteriorating patient to complete elective sedation steps.

Adenosine is a possible immediate adjunct for a regular narrow rhythm, not permission to delay available cardioversion through prolonged pharmacological trials. Unsynchronized defibrillation follows a different pathway, including VF or pulseless VT; reassess immediately if the pulse is lost. After conversion, obtain a diagnostic ECG, review reversible causes and document the arrhythmia for definitive evaluation. Successful conversion treats the episode but does not establish the precise reentrant circuit or remove the need to address recurrence.

otherOptions.explanation: Vagal maneuvers are appropriate initial treatment for suitable stable regular SVT. Persistent profound shock and altered mentation attributable to the rhythm make repeated attempts an inappropriate reason to delay cardioversion.

Diltiazem can treat selected stable narrow-complex tachycardias. In severe hypotension it can further compromise pressure, and waiting for drug effect delays definitive treatment of the unstable rhythm.

Adenosine can be considered for regular narrow-complex tachycardia while immediate cardioversion is being arranged. Completing an escalating sequence is not a prerequisite when profound instability persists and cardioversion is ready.

questions.question: An alert, hemodynamically stable adult has regular narrow-complex SVT and can cooperate with straining and repositioning. Which vagal maneuver best matches the method supported by the REVERT trial?
options: Supine positioning and passive leg elevation without a preceding strain
The same strain while remaining semirecumbent throughout recovery
A standardized semirecumbent strain followed immediately by supine repositioning and passive leg elevation
A standardized strain followed by standing upright during recovery
questions.explanation:
Modified Valsalva Maneuver for Stable SVT

Correct answer: A standardized semirecumbent strain followed immediately by supine repositioning and passive leg elevation

Use the Tested Sequence

**REVERT used a strain of ==40 mmHg for 15 seconds== from a semirecumbent position, followed immediately by supine repositioning and passive leg elevation.** The legs were raised to about ==45 degrees for 15 seconds== before returning to the semirecumbent position.

The postural change augments venous return during recovery and enhances the vagal response. Use supervised assistance and a practical method of standardizing the strain rather than asking for an unmeasured brief breath hold.

Select a patient who is stable, cooperative and able to perform the maneuver and reposition safely. Shock or severe deterioration calls for the unstable-tachycardia pathway rather than repeated maneuver attempts.

Interpret the Trial and the Rhythm Response

**In REVERT, conversion to sinus rhythm occurred in 43% with the modified maneuver versus 17% with the standard maneuver.** The primary endpoint was restoration of sinus rhythm at one minute, not long-term prevention of recurrence.

The intervention was studied in suitable adults with SVT; its findings should not be generalized to AF, flutter or every critically ill patient. AV nodal slowing can reveal atrial activity without actually terminating an atrial tachyarrhythmia.

Record ECG during the attempt and verify the resulting rhythm and perfusion. If an appropriate maneuver fails, monitored adenosine is a usual next option for regular narrow-complex SVT, followed by other treatment according to contraindications and response. Teach a safe self-management plan only after the diagnosis and individual suitability are established. This technique does not require carotid sinus pressure, and carotid massage has a different risk assessment. An initially successful vagal response does not uniquely distinguish AVNRT from AVRT.

Supine positioning and passive leg elevation without a preceding strain: Passive leg elevation alters venous return but is not the tested modified Valsalva sequence by itself. The standardized strain and immediate recovery-phase positioning are both components of the intervention.

The same strain while remaining semirecumbent throughout recovery: A standard Valsalva can terminate AV-node-dependent SVT, but remaining semirecumbent omits the postural modification that improved conversion in REVERT.

A standardized strain followed by standing upright during recovery: Upright recovery does not reproduce the increased venous return of the tested supine leg-raise sequence. It can also provoke presyncope and is not the REVERT intervention.

questions.question: A stable adult has regular narrow-complex SVT despite an appropriate vagal maneuver. There is no bronchospasm, transplant history or relevant interacting medication, and a proximal peripheral IV is available. Under the AHA 2025 algorithm, which initial regimen is appropriate?
options: 6 mg rapid IV push followed immediately by saline flush; 12 mg if needed
3 mg rapid IV push followed by saline flush; 6 mg if needed
6 mg by slow IV injection over several minutes; 12 mg if needed
12 mg rapid IV push followed by saline flush as the standard first dose
questions.explanation:
Adenosine Delivery for Regular Narrow-Complex SVT

Correct answer: 6 mg rapid IV push followed immediately by saline flush; 12 mg if needed

Short Duration Requires Rapid Delivery

**The AHA adult algorithm uses ==6 mg rapid IV push== with an immediate saline flush, followed by ==12 mg== if needed.** The rapid-bolus product label describes delivery over ==1–2 seconds== and reassessment before repeat dosing.

Adenosine transiently suppresses AV nodal conduction through adenosine-receptor effects. Rapid cellular uptake and metabolism give it a circulating half-life of less than ten seconds, making line position and technique clinically important.

Use continuous ECG recording, monitoring and resuscitation readiness. Explain the expected brief flushing, chest discomfort or sense of dyspnea while remaining alert to prolonged conduction disturbance or genuine bronchospasm.

Reassess the Response Before Escalating

**Termination is common in AV-node-dependent reentry, but a ventricular pause alone is not conversion.** Continuing flutter or atrial tachycardia may become visible during temporary AV block.

Check delivery if no expected effect occurs and review methylxanthine exposure, which can antagonize adenosine. Do not assume that every failure is a resistant reentrant circuit requiring repeated larger doses.

Dipyridamole potentiates adenosine, while carbamazepine can increase AV block; transplantation and central administration can also increase sensitivity and call for a modified approach. Avoid indiscriminate use in irregular or polymorphic wide-complex rhythms and suspected pre-excited AF. Hemodynamic deterioration changes the pathway to prompt electrical treatment. The regimen here is for bolus termination of suitable SVT, not the continuous infusion used in pharmacological stress testing; those indications must not be interchanged.

3 mg rapid IV push followed by saline flush; 6 mg if needed: A reduced starting dose may be appropriate in selected circumstances with enhanced adenosine effect or central delivery. Those circumstances are not supplied, and this is not the standard adult peripheral regimen in the named algorithm.

6 mg by slow IV injection over several minutes; 12 mg if needed: Adenosine is rapidly removed from the circulation. Slow administration can prevent an effective concentration from reaching the AV node; rapid bolus delivery and immediate flushing are essential to the intended effect.

12 mg rapid IV push followed by saline flush as the standard first dose: Twelve milligrams is the usual subsequent dose after an ineffective initial 6-mg bolus in the named algorithm. It should not replace the standard initial dose without a specific justified protocol or circumstance.

AHA adult advanced life support guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1161/CIR.0000000000001376

Adenosine rapid-bolus injection prescribing information — https://www.dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/drugInfo.cfm?setid=91a601ab-d3cc-4013-9108-1b5432476076

questions.question: A stable adult with regular narrow-complex SVT has persistent diffuse wheeze during an acute asthma exacerbation. Vagal maneuvers have failed. Which factor most directly argues against the usual next adenosine bolus?
options: Recent caffeine exposure
Active bronchospasm with risk of worsening airflow obstruction
Concurrent dipyridamole treatment
A history of transient flushing during a previous dose
questions.explanation:
Adenosine Precautions and Drug Interactions

Correct answer: Active bronchospasm with risk of worsening airflow obstruction

Distinguish Expected Dyspnea From Bronchospasm

**Adenosine can provoke clinically important bronchoconstriction and should be avoided in active bronchospasm.** Brief subjective dyspnea after a dose is common, but it does not justify dismissing wheeze or worsening respiratory distress.

The rapid-bolus prescribing information distinguishes bronchospastic disease from obstructive lung disease without bronchoconstriction, where caution is still required. Interpret the current respiratory phenotype rather than relying only on a diagnostic label.

Significant sinus-node dysfunction or second-/third-degree AV block without functioning pacing protection also raises concern because adenosine suppresses nodal activity. Assess the baseline rhythm and available rescue support.

Select an Alternative According to the Whole Patient

**Treat the respiratory exacerbation while selecting monitored SVT treatment compatible with pressure and ventricular function.** Verapamil or diltiazem may be considered in suitable stable patients; hypotension or HFrEF can make them inappropriate.

Beta blockade requires particular caution during active bronchospasm. If pharmacological options are contraindicated or ineffective, synchronized cardioversion is an established alternative, and deterioration requires urgent electrical management.

Review interactions before any later adenosine use: methylxanthines antagonize its effect, dipyridamole potentiates it, and carbamazepine can increase conduction block. A previous expected transient sensation is different from a serious adverse reaction. Do not respond to antagonist-associated nonresponse by unbounded dose escalation. Explain the selected treatment and document the actual respiratory findings, because future decisions should distinguish an episode of active bronchospasm from nonspecific discomfort during an otherwise tolerated dose.

Recent caffeine exposure: Caffeine antagonizes adenosine and can reduce efficacy. This interaction affects response assessment but is not the same direct reason to avoid adenosine as active bronchospasm.

Concurrent dipyridamole treatment: Dipyridamole potentiates adenosine and may require dose modification or an alternative strategy. It is an important interaction, but the question describes a separate direct respiratory hazard during active bronchospasm.

A history of transient flushing during a previous dose: Flushing is a common short-lived pharmacological effect and does not by itself establish a contraindication. It differs from objective bronchospasm or a documented serious hypersensitivity reaction.

questions.question: A stable adult has recurrent regular narrow-complex AV-node-dependent SVT despite vagal maneuvers and correctly delivered adenosine. BP is 128/76 mmHg, LVEF is normal, and there is no pre-excitation, conduction disease or recent IV beta blocker. A monitored pharmacological alternative is preferred. Which option is most appropriate?
options: IV diltiazem with continuous rhythm and blood-pressure monitoring
IV digoxin for prompt termination
IV amiodarone as the preferred next nodal treatment
Oral flecainide as the preferred immediate rescue
questions.explanation:
Alternative Treatment for Persistent Stable Regular SVT

Correct answer: IV diltiazem with continuous rhythm and blood-pressure monitoring

Confirm the Rhythm and the Hemodynamic Margin

**IV diltiazem or verapamil can treat suitable stable regular narrow-complex SVT when vagal maneuvers and adenosine are ineffective or unsuitable.** A beta blocker is another option in an appropriate clinical context.

Review the actual adenosine response and exclude a continuing atrial driver before assuming treatment-resistant AV-node-dependent reentry. Confirm QRS width, regularity and absence of pre-excited AF.

The preserved EF and adequate pressure here support use of a nondihydropyridine calcium-channel blocker. Hypotension, significant systolic dysfunction or an uncertain wide-complex rhythm changes that decision.

Dose and Monitor Diltiazem

**The IV label uses ==0.25 mg/kg over 2 minutes== as the initial bolus.** If response is inadequate, a second ==0.35 mg/kg over 2 minutes== can be given after ==15 minutes== according to the prescribing information.

Monitor for hypotension, bradycardia and AV block. Avoid uncritical combination with IV beta blockade because additive nodal and myocardial suppression can be clinically important.

Infusion regimens used for continuing AF rate control should not be assumed necessary after successful conversion of a reentrant SVT. If appropriate medication fails or is contraindicated, synchronized cardioversion is an established alternative even in a currently stable patient. Escalate promptly if perfusion deteriorates. Recurrent symptomatic AVNRT or AVRT warrants discussion of definitive electrophysiological assessment and ablation rather than an indefinite succession of emergency drug trials. Acute response alone does not fully determine the circuit or the best long-term strategy.

IV digoxin for prompt termination: Digoxin slows AV conduction and has selected rate-control roles, particularly in AF. Its slower and less predictable acute action makes it a poor substitute for rapid termination of this recurrent regular SVT.

IV amiodarone as the preferred next nodal treatment: Amiodarone has roles in selected ventricular or atrial arrhythmias and complex substrates. Its broader toxicity and slower action make it less suitable than a standard AV nodal agent for this uncomplicated stable narrow-complex setting.

Oral flecainide as the preferred immediate rescue: Flecainide can have selected specialist roles after structural and ischemic assessment. Oral administration is not the usual immediate monitored alternative when an established AV nodal treatment can address the acute episode.

questions.question: An adult with prior myocardial infarction has regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia at 170/min and BP 112/70 mmHg. The mechanism remains uncertain after initial ECG review. Which proposed approach is least appropriate?
options: Use an appropriate monitored antiarrhythmic strategy for tolerated monomorphic VT
Obtain expert assessment while preparing synchronized cardioversion if deterioration occurs
Give IV verapamil as an empirical test for SVT with aberrancy
Consider monitored adenosine if the rhythm remains stable, regular and monomorphic
questions.explanation:
Uncertain Wide-Complex Tachycardia and AV Nodal Drugs

Correct answer: Give IV verapamil as an empirical test for SVT with aberrancy

Hemodynamic Tolerance Does Not Exclude VT

**A patient can remain awake with an adequate pressure during ventricular tachycardia.** Previous infarction increases concern for scar-related VT, so stability must not be mistaken for proof of SVT.

Assess a 12-lead ECG, baseline conduction and available rhythm history. AV dissociation, capture or fusion beats support VT, but their absence does not exclude it.

An empirical verapamil challenge can cause severe hypotension or collapse when the rhythm is VT. AHA 2025 advises against verapamil and diltiazem for undifferentiated wide-complex tachycardia.

Use a Strategy Compatible With the Uncertainty

**A stable regular monomorphic rhythm can undergo expert evaluation and selected monitored antiarrhythmic treatment.** Synchronized cardioversion is appropriate for instability or when other treatment fails or is unsuitable.

Adenosine may be considered in stable regular monomorphic wide-complex tachycardia to help diagnosis or treat an AV-node-dependent rhythm. Record the response and maintain immediate rescue capability.

Do not extend this exception to irregular wide-complex tachycardia, suspected pre-excited AF or polymorphic VT. Known verapamil-sensitive fascicular VT is a specific specialist diagnosis and does not justify verapamil in an undifferentiated postinfarction rhythm. Distinguish the acute protection decision from later mechanism confirmation; a VT-compatible initial approach reduces the risk of harmful misclassification while additional evidence is obtained. Reassess pulse and perfusion continuously, because loss of pulse requires the cardiac-arrest pathway.

Use an appropriate monitored antiarrhythmic strategy for tolerated monomorphic VT: An uncertain wide-complex rhythm, particularly with prior infarction, warrants a VT-compatible strategy. Drug selection must account for QT, HF, blood pressure and contraindications rather than assuming all agents are equivalent.

Obtain expert assessment while preparing synchronized cardioversion if deterioration occurs: Current stability permits a focused diagnostic and treatment assessment with rescue readiness. It does not establish a supraventricular mechanism, and cardioversion should be available if the rhythm becomes poorly tolerated.

Consider monitored adenosine if the rhythm remains stable, regular and monomorphic: AHA 2025 permits consideration of adenosine for diagnosis or treatment in this restricted phenotype. It is not permission to use adenosine in unstable, irregular or polymorphic wide-complex tachycardia.

questions.question: At 24 weeks of pregnancy, a patient has abrupt regular narrow-complex SVT at 190/min. BP and perfusion are normal, the heart is structurally normal and an appropriate vagal maneuver has failed. There is no bronchospasm or pre-excitation. Which next treatment is preferred?
options: IV verapamil before attempting adenosine
IV metoprolol before attempting adenosine
Monitored IV adenosine for acute termination
Immediate catheter ablation as the next acute treatment
questions.explanation:
Acute Regular SVT During Pregnancy

Correct answer: Monitored IV adenosine for acute termination

Use a Stability-Based Sequence

**ESC 2025 recommends vagal maneuvers and IV adenosine for suitable hemodynamically stable SVT during pregnancy.** Maternal stabilization benefits fetal perfusion; pregnancy does not justify leaving sustained symptomatic tachycardia untreated.

The ESC pathway uses adenosine boluses within a 6–18-mg framework. Local resuscitation protocols may specify a 6-mg initial dose followed by 12 mg; state the framework rather than implying every organization has an identical upper bolus regimen.

Confirm regularity, QRS width and absence of contraindications. Record the response because AV nodal slowing can reveal an atrial tachyarrhythmia rather than terminate it.

Escalate Without Delaying Maternal Resuscitation

**Synchronized cardioversion is indicated when SVT causes hemodynamic instability during pregnancy.** Arrange fetal assessment and appropriate monitoring when feasible, without delaying urgent maternal treatment.

Selected beta blockers, commonly metoprolol, or verapamil may be used when first-line measures fail or are unsuitable. Consider maternal pressure, ventricular function, bronchospasm and fetal effects; atenolol is avoided in the ESC pregnancy framework.

For recurrence, coordinate cardiology, obstetric and anesthesia expertise as appropriate. Balance frequency and tolerance against drug exposure, and consider an experienced low-radiation ablation program for refractory disease. Elective definitive treatment before a planned pregnancy may be preferable in recurrent symptomatic SVT. Do not equate an effective acute bolus with a complete long-term plan, or extrapolate antiarrhythmic safety from nonpregnant adults without checking pregnancy-specific guidance. Reassess reversible triggers and document the rhythm for subsequent decisions.

IV verapamil before attempting adenosine: Verapamil is an alternative in selected circumstances, with attention to maternal pressure and ventricular function. It is not preferred over adenosine for the supplied uncomplicated stable AV-node-dependent SVT.

IV metoprolol before attempting adenosine: Metoprolol can be used in selected pregnancy-associated SVT when needed, but adenosine is the preferred first medication after failed vagal maneuvers in this suitable stable presentation.

Immediate catheter ablation as the next acute treatment: Low- or zero-fluoroscopy ablation can be considered for selected recurrent drug-refractory or poorly tolerated arrhythmias during pregnancy. A first suitable drug trial is appropriate for this stable episode rather than proceeding directly to an invasive intervention.

ESC cardiovascular disease and pregnancy guideline, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehaf193

questions.question: A patient has near-continuous focal AT at 140/min and new global LV dysfunction with LVEF 30%. Coronary and other initial etiological assessment is unrevealing. Tolerated medical treatment has not suppressed the tachycardia. Which strategy best addresses the suspected reversible driver?
options: Implant a primary-prevention ICD immediately before attempting rhythm control
Escalate rate control alone and defer rhythm treatment until EF normalizes
Refer for focal AT mapping and catheter ablation while treating HF and reassessing LV recovery
Use repeated cardioversion as the preferred durable strategy
questions.explanation:
Incessant Atrial Tachycardia and Arrhythmia-Induced Cardiomyopathy

Correct answer: Refer for focal AT mapping and catheter ablation while treating HF and reassessing LV recovery

A Modest Rate Can Still Produce Ventricular Dysfunction

**Arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy depends on rhythm burden and duration as well as rate.** An incessant AT at 140/min can be consequential even without extremely rapid paroxysms.

Assess other causes of LV dysfunction and the possibility that pre-existing myocardial disease contributes. Temporal association raises suspicion; improvement after effective rhythm treatment strengthens the attribution.

Document the rhythm burden, ventricular function and clinical HF status. A single office pulse after a brief slower period is insufficient evidence that the driver has been controlled.

Eliminate the Driver and Follow Recovery

**ESC SVT guidance recommends ablation for recurrent focal AT, especially when incessant or causing tachycardiomyopathy.** The EHRA multisociety AT consensus also supports ablation for incessant AT with arrhythmia-induced cardiomyopathy.

Use electrophysiological mapping to identify the source and assess anatomical risk. Treat congestion and provide appropriate HF therapy concurrently rather than waiting for ablation to address all hemodynamic consequences.

Reassess symptoms, rhythm burden and EF after treatment. Recovery can take weeks to months and may be incomplete when another cardiomyopathy coexists; avoid promising immediate normalization. Persistent dysfunction requires renewed etiological and device-risk assessment. AV-junction ablation with pacing is a selected fallback when atrial rhythm control is not feasible or effective, not the default substitute for an ablatable focal source. Discuss recurrence and procedural risks, and maintain follow-up even after an initially successful procedure because recurrent tachycardia can again impair ventricular function.

Implant a primary-prevention ICD immediately before attempting rhythm control: An ICD may later be indicated if ventricular dysfunction persists under the relevant criteria. Newly recognized dysfunction with a potentially reversible incessant arrhythmia requires treatment and reassessment rather than assuming an immediate permanent sudden-death indication.

Escalate rate control alone and defer rhythm treatment until EF normalizes: Rate treatment can help selected patients, but persistent tachycardia may itself prevent ventricular recovery. Waiting for EF normalization before addressing the documented driver reverses the necessary treatment sequence.

Use repeated cardioversion as the preferred durable strategy: Cardioversion may help selected acute atrial tachycardias, but an incessant focal source can recur promptly. Mapping and ablation offer a mechanism-directed durable strategy when the documented rhythm persists despite tolerated treatment.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

EHRA multisociety atrial tachycardia consensus, 2025 — https://doi.org/10.1093/europace/euaf324

questions.question: An electrophysiology study demonstrates a regular reentrant tachycardia using antegrade conduction through the AV node and His–Purkinje system, with retrograde return through an atrioventricular accessory pathway. Which classification is correct?
options: Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia
Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia
Atrial tachycardia with bystander pre-excitation
questions.explanation:
Orthodromic and Antidromic AV Reentry

Correct answer: Orthodromic AV reentrant tachycardia

Name the Circuit by Antegrade Activation

**Orthodromic AVRT conducts from atrium to ventricle through the AV node and His–Purkinje system, then returns through an accessory pathway.** Ventricular activation is usually narrow because the normal conduction system activates it.

Antidromic AVRT activates the ventricle antegradely through an accessory pathway and returns through the AV node or another accessory pathway. Its QRS is pre-excited and wide.

QRS width supports the mechanism but is not sufficient alone: orthodromic AVRT can develop bundle-branch aberrancy, while wide-complex tachycardia has several other causes.

Distinguish Pathway Participation From Pathway Presence

**A manifest accessory pathway can coexist with a rhythm that does not use it as a necessary circuit limb.** AF, flutter, focal AT or AVNRT can conduct through a bystander pathway.

Electrophysiological maneuvers establish whether pathway conduction is required for the tachycardia. That distinction determines the mechanism and helps select the ablation target.

Acute treatment depends on stability, regularity, QRS pattern and whether pre-excited AF is possible. A nodal-blocking approach suitable for ordinary regular orthodromic AVRT must not be transferred to irregular pre-excited AF. For recurrent symptomatic AVRT, accessory-pathway ablation is a definitive option after discussion of pathway location, procedural risk and patient preferences. A clear circuit description is more informative than using the presence of a delta wave as a general label for every episode of palpitations.

Mechanism | Antegrade limb | Retrograde limb | Usual QRS

Orthodromic AVRT | AV node–His–Purkinje | Accessory pathway | Narrow unless aberrancy

Antidromic AVRT | Accessory pathway | AV node or another pathway | Wide and pre-excited

Typical AVNRT | Slow nodal pathway | Fast nodal pathway | Usually narrow

Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Antidromic AVRT uses an accessory pathway for antegrade ventricular activation, producing a pre-excited QRS. The antegrade limb here is the normal AV nodal and His–Purkinje route.

Typical AV nodal reentrant tachycardia: Typical AVNRT uses functionally distinct nodal pathways rather than requiring an atrioventricular accessory pathway and the ventricle in the circuit. The demonstrated extranodal retrograde limb establishes AVRT.

Atrial tachycardia with bystander pre-excitation: An atrial tachycardia can activate the ventricle through a bystander accessory pathway without using it to sustain the atrial rhythm. Here the pathway is an essential retrograde limb of the demonstrated reentrant circuit.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent abrupt regular narrow-complex tachycardia despite a normal PR interval and no delta wave on several sinus ECGs. EPS establishes an accessory pathway that conducts from ventricle to atrium but not antegradely. Which statement is correct?
options: The pathway creates the same rapid pre-excited AF mechanism as a short-refractory antegrade pathway
Absence of a delta wave makes the demonstrated pathway incapable of sustaining AVRT
The pathway can provide the antegrade limb of antidromic AVRT
The pathway can sustain orthodromic AVRT without producing resting ventricular pre-excitation
questions.explanation:
Concealed Accessory Pathways

Correct answer: The pathway can sustain orthodromic AVRT without producing resting ventricular pre-excitation

Concealed Refers to the Direction of Conduction

**A concealed accessory pathway conducts retrogradely and therefore does not produce a delta wave in sinus rhythm.** It can nevertheless participate as the return limb of orthodromic AVRT.

During tachycardia, the AV node and His–Purkinje system activate the ventricle antegradely, and the pathway returns activation to the atrium. The usual narrow QRS does not imply absence of an accessory connection.

Distinguish a proven retrograde-only pathway from intermittent manifest pre-excitation. A normal single ECG in the latter setting may reflect changing competition or pathway conduction rather than permanent absence of antegrade capability.

questions.explanation:
Recognition of Pre-Excited Atrial Fibrillation

Correct answer: Atrial fibrillation with antegrade accessory-pathway conduction

Variable Ventricular Activation Signals a Different Emergency

**Pre-excited AF can deliver rapid irregular atrial impulses to the ventricle through an accessory pathway.** Changing competition between AV nodal and accessory conduction produces varying QRS width and morphology.

A prior short PR and delta wave establish manifest pre-excitation as a relevant substrate. The acute tracing must still be interpreted directly; not every wide rhythm in a patient with an accessory pathway is AVRT.

A pathway with a short antegrade refractory period can permit dangerously rapid ventricular responses and degeneration to VF. Assess pulse and perfusion continuously rather than waiting for a particular displayed average rate.

Avoid the Ordinary AF Rate-Control Reflex

**AV nodal blocking drugs are contraindicated in pre-excited AF because ventricular acceleration and VF can occur.** The US 2023 guideline includes adenosine, beta blockers, verapamil, diltiazem, digoxin and amiodarone in this warning.

Unstable patients require immediate electrical cardioversion. In suitable stable patients, IV procainamide or ibutilide can be used with monitoring as alternatives to electrical conversion.

If polymorphic VT or VF is present, follow the appropriate unsynchronized-defibrillation pathway; an uncertain rapidly deteriorating wide-complex rhythm must not be exposed to empirical nodal blockade. After stabilization, refer for accessory-pathway assessment and ablation. The crucial distinction is between regular AV-node-dependent reentry, where nodal interruption can terminate the circuit, and irregular antegrade pathway conduction during AF, where that same drug strategy can be hazardous.

Antidromic AV reentrant tachycardia: Antidromic AVRT produces pre-excited wide complexes, but its reentrant cycle is ordinarily regular. The very irregular intervals and changing degrees of pre-excitation favor AF conducting through both available routes.

AF with fixed bundle-branch aberrancy: AF with bundle-branch disease can be irregular and wide, but fixed aberrancy generally preserves a more consistent conduction pattern. Known manifest pre-excitation and extreme variable ventricular activation raise concern for accessory conduction.

Polymorphic ventricular tachycardia: Polymorphic VT is an important dangerous wide-complex alternative. Here the prior delta wave and irregularly variable pre-excited pattern specifically support AF with accessory conduction, although diagnostic uncertainty must still be managed safely.

questions.explanation:
Pharmacological Conversion of Stable Pre-Excited AF

Correct answer: Procainamide or ibutilide with continuous monitoring and cardioversion readiness

Select a Pathway-Compatible Drug

**US 2023 recommends IV procainamide or ibutilide for suitable stable pre-excited AF as alternatives to electrical cardioversion.** Stability permits consideration of drugs; it does not make conventional AV nodal rate control safe.

Electrical conversion remains an appropriate option and becomes urgent with attributable hypotension, shock, altered mentation, ischemia or acute HF. Do not prolong a drug infusion while deterioration develops.

Review QT, ventricular function, pressure, electrolytes, renal status and recent antiarrhythmics before selecting treatment. The two agents are alternatives, not a routine sequential combination.

Dose With ECG and Hemodynamic Limits

**The AHA wide-QRS algorithm lists procainamide ==20–50 mg/min== to suppression or a stopping limit.** Stop for hypotension, QRS widening greater than 50% or a cumulative ==17 mg/kg==; avoid prolonged QT or significant HF.

Ibutilide labelling uses ==1 mg over 10 minutes== at weight 60 kg or greater, or ==0.01 mg/kg== below 60 kg. If the arrhythmia persists, a second equal 10-minute infusion may begin ==10 minutes after the first infusion ends== when otherwise eligible; stop for conversion, sustained or nonsustained VT, or marked QT/QTc prolongation.

Correct potassium and magnesium and monitor for QT-related polymorphic VT. Continue ECG monitoring for at least four hours after ibutilide or until QTc returns to baseline, longer if arrhythmia occurs. Avoid stacking other QT-prolonging antiarrhythmics without specialist guidance. These are monitored hospital regimens, not unsupervised rescue prescriptions. After conversion, assess stroke prevention as appropriate and arrange definitive pathway treatment; successful acute conversion does not remove the substrate for recurrent rapid pre-excited AF.

Adenosine with continuous monitoring: Adenosine can terminate regular AV-node-dependent SVT and has a limited role in stable regular monomorphic wide tachycardia. Irregular pre-excited AF is a different phenotype in which nodal blockade is hazardous.

Amiodarone with continuous monitoring: IV amiodarone has roles in AF without pre-excitation and in other arrhythmias. It is contraindicated for pre-excited AF in the named guideline because ventricular acceleration and VF have been reported.

Diltiazem with continuous monitoring: Diltiazem can control ventricular rate in ordinary AF when pressure and EF permit. It blocks the AV node without providing the required safe accessory-pathway strategy in pre-excited AF.

questions.question: During EPS for manifest pre-excitation, induced AF has a shortest pre-excited R–R interval of 220 ms. Which interpretation best matches ESC 2019 risk stratification?
options: The measurement primarily establishes slow retrograde pathway conduction
The measurement is reassuring because the average ventricular rate is lower
Risk cannot be assessed until a spontaneous clinical AF episode is recorded
The pathway has a high-risk antegrade conduction property supporting ablation discussion
questions.explanation:
High-Risk Accessory-Pathway Conduction

Correct answer: The pathway has a high-risk antegrade conduction property supporting ablation discussion

Use the Correct Interval and Threshold

**SPERRI is the shortest pre-excited R–R interval during AF.** ESC 2019 identifies ==SPERRI ≤250 ms== as a high-risk accessory-pathway feature; 220 ms clearly meets that criterion.

Measure genuinely pre-excited complexes and distinguish artefact, fusion and non-pre-excited conduction. A short interval shows that the pathway can deliver closely spaced impulses to the ventricular myocardium.

The pathway effective refractory period is a separate measurement; ==antegrade AP ERP ≤250 ms== is another high-risk feature. The two tests address related conduction properties but are not interchangeable labels.

Integrate the Electrophysiological Findings

**Multiple pathways and inducible accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia also contribute to the ESC high-risk framework.** Catecholamine challenge can expose conduction properties not apparent under baseline conditions.

High-risk findings support catheter ablation after discussion of benefits and procedural risk, including AV-block risk near the septal conduction system. A favorable current symptom history does not erase a documented rapid pathway.

Conversely, a threshold predicts risk rather than guaranteeing VF in an individual. Explain uncertainty without describing observation as equivalent protection against an established high-risk substrate. Assess occupation, athletics, prior syncope and structural disease as part of the overall decision. Do not confuse a retrograde-only concealed pathway with a manifest pathway capable of rapid antegrade AF conduction. After successful ablation, verify pathway elimination and arrange follow-up appropriate to symptoms and procedural findings.

EPS finding | ESC 2019 high-risk feature

Shortest pre-excited RR during AF | ≤250 ms

Antegrade accessory-pathway ERP | ≤250 ms

Pathway number | Multiple accessory pathways

Inducibility | Accessory-pathway-mediated tachycardia at baseline or catecholamine challenge

The measurement primarily establishes slow retrograde pathway conduction: The pre-excited R–R interval during AF reflects antegrade delivery to the ventricle. Slowly conducting retrograde pathways are relevant to PJRT but do not explain this rapid antegrade property.

The measurement is reassuring because the average ventricular rate is lower: SPERRI measures the fastest demonstrated pre-excited ventricular conduction rather than the average rate. Longer intervening intervals do not neutralize a documented very short pre-excited interval.

Risk cannot be assessed until a spontaneous clinical AF episode is recorded: Induced AF during a properly conducted EPS can assess pathway conduction. A spontaneous dangerous episode is not required before acting on a qualifying high-risk electrophysiological finding.

questions.question: An asymptomatic commercial pilot has manifest ventricular pre-excitation. During exercise the delta wave gradually becomes less obvious, without an abrupt documented transition to fully normal conduction. Which next approach best matches ESC 2019 guidance?
options: Use ambulatory monitoring alone and investigate further only after symptoms occur
Declare the pathway low risk because pre-excitation becomes less visible with exercise
Refer for EPS-based pathway risk stratification, including appropriate catecholamine assessment
Proceed to ablation without characterizing pathway properties or location
questions.explanation:
Asymptomatic Pre-Excitation in a High-Risk Occupation

Correct answer: Refer for EPS-based pathway risk stratification, including appropriate catecholamine assessment

Occupational Consequences Change the Evaluation

**ESC 2019 recommends EPS risk stratification for asymptomatic pre-excitation in high-risk occupations and competitive athletes.** The clinical concern includes both pathway-mediated sudden-death risk and the consequences of an arrhythmic event during the activity.

Assess prior overlooked palpitations or syncope, family and structural history, and the actual ECG evidence. Asymptomatic means no recognized clinical event, not proof of a pathway incapable of rapid conduction.

EPS evaluates antegrade refractoriness, pre-excited AF conduction, inducible AVRT and multiple pathways, with catecholamine assessment when appropriate.

Understand the Limits of Exercise Reassurance

**Abrupt complete loss of pre-excitation suggests less robust antegrade pathway conduction, but gradual fading is not the same observation.** Increasing AV nodal contribution can obscure a delta wave while pathway conduction persists.

Intermittent pre-excitation and a reassuring exercise result do not guarantee absence of high-risk invasive properties. A prospective 2024 study found limited sensitivity of low-risk exercise findings for excluding short SPERRI or AP ERP.

Discuss ablation when EPS identifies high-risk properties and weigh septal AV-block risk, patient preference and applicable occupational assessment. Selected genuinely low-risk patients can be followed, but the decision should follow an adequate evaluation rather than the visual disappearance of a small delta wave at peak exercise. Do not portray noninvasive testing as useless; it supplies evidence whose limitations matter when the consequence of a missed high-risk pathway is substantial.

questions.question: A patient has recurrent symptomatic typical AVNRT requiring emergency treatment despite an acceptable trial of medication. EPS confirms the mechanism, and the patient chooses definitive treatment. Which ablation target is generally preferred?
options: The compact AV node followed by permanent pacing
The AV nodal fast-pathway region as the routine first target
An atrioventricular accessory pathway at the earliest retrograde atrial site
The AV nodal slow-pathway region with preservation of normal AV conduction
questions.explanation:
Slow-Pathway Ablation for Recurrent AVNRT

Correct answer: The AV nodal slow-pathway region with preservation of normal AV conduction

Treat the Demonstrated Reentrant Substrate

**Slow-pathway modification is the usual ablation strategy for symptomatic recurrent AVNRT.** It interrupts the substrate for reentry while preserving clinically adequate antegrade AV conduction.

Typical slow–fast AVNRT uses slow antegrade and fast retrograde nodal conduction. The anatomy is approached through inferior nodal extensions rather than treating every early atrial signal as an accessory pathway.

Ablation offers high success, but procedural risk is not zero. Discuss AV block requiring pacing, vascular complications, recurrence and the alternatives in terms appropriate to the patient and center.

Use an Appropriate Procedural Endpoint

**Noninducibility of the clinical AVNRT is an important success endpoint.** A junctional rhythm during RF delivery is a useful procedural observation but does not alone prove durable success.

Residual dual nodal physiology does not automatically justify progressively hazardous lesions when the clinical arrhythmia is no longer inducible. The multicenter endpoint study cautions against unnecessary attempts to abolish every residual nodal feature.

Cryoablation can reduce the risk of permanent AV injury in selected settings but may carry more recurrence than RF; energy choice depends on anatomy and operator assessment. Observation remains reasonable for selected minimally symptomatic patients with rare brief episodes, while nodal drugs are options when ablation is unwanted or unsuitable. The recurrent emergency-treated presentation here supports definitive treatment. Follow symptoms after the procedure because palpitations can reflect ectopy or another rhythm rather than recurrent AVNRT; document the rhythm before assuming procedural failure.

The compact AV node followed by permanent pacing: AV-junction ablation with pacing has selected roles in refractory rate control, especially atrial arrhythmias. It intentionally creates dependence on pacing and is disproportionate when slow-pathway modification can treat AVNRT while preserving conduction.

The AV nodal fast-pathway region as the routine first target: Fast-pathway ablation can interrupt nodal reentry but has a greater risk of damaging essential AV conduction. Contemporary routine treatment targets the slow pathway rather than sacrificing the fast pathway.

An atrioventricular accessory pathway at the earliest retrograde atrial site: Accessory-pathway ablation treats AVRT when pathway participation is established. An early retrograde atrial signal during confirmed AVNRT does not by itself establish an extranodal accessory connection.

ESC supraventricular tachycardia guideline, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1093/eurheartj/ehz467

ACC/AHA/HRS adult SVT guideline, 2015 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacc.2015.08.856

Multicenter study of slow-pathway ablation endpoints, 2019 — https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacep.2018.09.012

questions.question: A patient with recurrent symptomatic AVRT chooses ablation. Mapping locates an anteroseptal accessory pathway close to His recordings. Which counseling statement is most appropriate?
options: The AV-block risk is the same as for a left lateral free-wall pathway
Ablation can be effective, but proximity to normal conduction increases AV-block risk and affects energy and strategy selection
